title: Salsabila and the Sparkling Sea
blurb: Strange blue lights dance on the water near the island, and nobody agrees what they are. Salsabila decides to find out.

chapters.title: Lights on the Water
chapters.text:
The island of Pulau Lerang was so small that Salsabila could walk around it before lunch. Her grandmother, Nenek, sold dried fish at the harbour, and every evening Salsabila sat on the end of the old wooden jetty, watching the sky turn orange.

On the third night of the school holidays, she noticed something strange. Far out beyond the rocks, tiny blue lights flickered on the black water. They did not move like boat lamps. They sparkled and faded, like stars falling into the sea.

"Nenek, come and see!" she called.

Nenek stood on the jetty for a long time, her hand shading her eyes. "I have lived here for seventy years," she said slowly. "I have never seen that."

Salsabila's best friend Galih came running along the planks. "The fishermen are talking about it," he panted. "They say it is a bad sign."

chapters.title: What the Elders Said
chapters.text:
The next morning, the whole harbour was buzzing. Pak Haji, the oldest fisherman, sat on an upturned boat with his arms crossed. "In my grandfather's time," he said, "there were lights like these before a great wave. We must not take the boats out."

Some men nodded. Others shook their heads. "It is only a trick of the moon," said a young fisherman called Rudi.

Salsabila listened carefully. She liked Pak Haji, but she also liked finding things out for herself. At school, her science teacher Bu Dewi often said, "Do not argue about a mystery. Collect evidence."

"Galih," she said quietly, "I do not think the lights are a warning. I think they are something we can study. Do you have your notebook?"

Galih grinned. "I always do."

chapters.title: A Plan for Midnight
chapters.text:
That afternoon, the friends sat on the jetty with a pencil and a chart. Galih had noticed that the lights had appeared at about nine o'clock, and again around midnight.

"If we want to see them closely," said Salsabila, "we must go out. We need a boat."

"Nenek's little canoe has no engine," said Galih. "We can paddle quietly. That is better, anyway. A motor might scare away whatever it is."

Salsabila wrote a list: torch, notebook, a glass jar with a lid, two life jackets, a rope and a thermos of warm tea. She frowned. "We need to tell an adult," she said. "Rule number one, even for scientists."

So she asked Nenek, who thought about it for a long time. "You may go," she said at last, "but you will stay close to the jetty light, and I will sit at the end with my torch."

chapters.title: The Water That Glowed
chapters.text:
At ten minutes to midnight, the friends pushed the canoe from the beach. The sea was dark and calm. They paddled slowly, and each time the paddle dipped, something wonderful happened. The water around the blade burst into a cloud of tiny blue sparks, like glitter lit from inside.

"Look!" whispered Galih. He trailed his hand through the water. Glowing swirls streamed from his fingers.

Salsabila held her breath. "There is no ghost here," she said softly. "The sea itself is glowing."

She dipped her jar and lifted it. Inside the water, a thousand tiny dots glowed each time the jar moved, and dimmed when it stood still. "They shine when they are disturbed," she said. "That is why the lights flashed near the rocks. The waves were moving them."

Far away on the jetty, a torch blinked twice. Nenek was watching.

chapters.title: Bu Dewi Explains
chapters.text:
In the morning, Salsabila brought the jar to school and showed it to Bu Dewi. The teacher put a few drops under the microscope and her eyebrows rose. "Beautiful," she said. "These are called dinoflagellates. They are single-celled living things, so small that you cannot see one without a microscope. But when many of them gather, they make the water glow."

"Why do they glow?" asked Galih.

"Scientists think the light is a defence," said Bu Dewi. "When a tiny animal tries to eat them, the flash may attract a bigger animal that eats the attacker. This glowing is called bioluminescence. Many deep-sea creatures also make their own light."

"So, is it a bad sign?" asked Salsabila.

"It is a sign that the sea is alive," said Bu Dewi. "Large groups like this often appear when the water is warm and full of nutrients. It will pass in a few days."

chapters.title: Keeping the Secret
chapters.text:
By evening, the news had spread across Pulau Lerang. Pak Haji listened to Salsabila's explanation, stroking his chin. At last he said, "I am old and I have lived by the old stories. But today I have learned something new. That is a good day."

The fishermen laughed, and some of them clapped Salsabila on the back. Rudi gave her a lopsided grin. "You win," he said. "It was not the moon."

A few days later, the glow faded, just as Bu Dewi had said. But visitors had already begun to arrive in small boats, eager to see the sparkling sea.

At the harbour meeting, Salsabila stood up. "It is lovely to share the sea," she said. "But we must keep it clean. No rubbish, no loud engines, no chemicals. Remember that the sea is a home for living things."

Everyone agreed. That night, the sea was quiet and dark again, and Salsabila smiled. She knew where to look for stars.
